notes.reason: The claim really is the author's own. He writes plainly of Faggella: "How does he get around the problem where every word you pick for the ultimate thing has some stupid implication if you think about it for five seconds? He invents his own new word: 'potentia'." The note is also factually right. Potentia is ordinary Latin for force, power and ability, and Faggella's own essay presents it as Spinoza's term, writing "Spinoza has a word for this as well" before "Potentia is all the possible ways that the conatus behooves its aim of persisting". I fetched both sources and both say what the accepted quotes say they say. The problem is that the correction does not matter. The sentence is a one-line jab inside a 35,000-character essay about the ideology of successionism, and the author's actual argument is that Faggella reaches for an unfamiliar grand-sounding word to dodge the reductio that catches "complexity", "negentropy" and "intelligence". That argument survives the correction untouched, and in fact an old borrowed word fits the author's mockery of "picking random fancy-sounding science words" even better than a coinage would. Sending a Latin dictionary link to correct a rhetorical aside is the kind of pedantry that makes a careful author dismiss the whole batch, so this one should not go out.
